facts.text: Hope is thought to have been around 15 years old at the time of her death.
Hope is thought to have been around 15 years old at the time of her death.
Hope was likely born sometime around 1876.
On the morning of 25 March 1891, Hope became stranded on a sandy ridge called Swantons Bank at the mouth of Wexford Harbour.
It is uncertain why Hope ended up trapped on the sandbank.
Bad weather might have caused her to lose her bearings, or she may still have been weak from the effort of raising a calf.
Ned Wickham eventually killed Hope to save her from further suffering by plunging an improvised harpoon under one of her flippers.
Hope's carcass was auctioned off by the Receiver of Wreck, a role normally associated with salvaging shipwrecks.
The auction raised £111.
Whales have been deemed 'royal fish' under UK law since 1324, meaning they automatically belong to the reigning monarch and the government acting on their behalf.
William Armstrong extracted almost 3,000 litres of oil from Hope.
William Armstrong sold the skeleton to the museum for £250, which the museum says is the equivalent of over £28,000 today.
The pattern of isotopes and hormones in Hope's baleen is consistent with what researchers would expect to see in a pregnant whale, though the museum says it is impossible to be certain.
After 42 years in storage, Hope was finally put on display in 1934.
Hope's 1934 display followed the work of the museum's taxidermist and technical assistant Percy Stammwitz.
The centrepiece of the project was the suspension of a 25m blue whale skeleton, since named 'Hope', from the Victorian wrought iron roof girders.
The Hintze Hall was designed by architect Alfred Waterhouse in 1881.
The skeleton was displayed in the Mammal Hall from 1934 before being moved to the museum's main Hintze Hall in 2017.
In Hintze Hall, Hope replaced Dippy, a cast of a diplodocus skeleton.
